arm_policy_hint.auto_bypass: Excluded and announced; included again by itself once closed.
arm_policy_hint.arm_after_closing: Arming waits, after the exit delay, until it closes. It fails if it stays open too long.

overview.technical_banner: Technical alarm: {zones}. A separate channel: arming does not affect it and disarming does not clear it. It clears once acknowledged and the sensors are back to normal.

overview.incident_hint: One incident gathers every zone of one alarm. Disarming also acknowledges it; arming does not.
overview.memory_banner_plain: Alarm memory in {area}. It clears when the area is disarmed or armed again.

areas.title: Areas
areas.reports_as_hint: What voice assistants and HomeKit see. Changes nothing about behaviour.
areas.entry_hint: For zones that do not set their own.
areas.exit_hint: Time to leave after arming, unless the scenario sets its own.
areas.perimeter_hint: The outer defence ring. An automatic rule never disarms a perimeter area, whatever the rule says.

zones.title: Zones
zones.no_areas: Create an area first: every zone belongs to one.
zones.entity_hint: Any sensor, door sensor, cover, lock, switch, person, event or tag.
zones.state_hint: Normally-closed and normally-open contact sensors behave in opposite ways. Open the door or walk past and watch the state.
zones.hysteresis_hint: A margin: after triggering, the value must come back past the threshold by this much before the zone counts as normal again. It stops a reading that hovers at the threshold from firing over and over.
zones.attribute_hint: Read this attribute instead of the state.
zones.tag_hint: A tag fires every time it is scanned.
zones.event_hint: Only this event triggers the zone.
zones.confirm: I have checked this against the real sensor
zones.confirm_hint: A wrong choice is a zone that never fires, found out during a break-in.
zones.unconfirmed_notice: This zone was brought across by an import, and its trigger is a proposal read from the sensor's type, not something anybody has checked. It stays switched off until you have: test the sensor, correct the trigger if it is wrong, tick the confirmation and switch the zone on.
zones.type_hint: A preset: it fills the fields below, which all stay editable.
zones.hold_hint: Empty: the global default. Counted from the end of the exit delay.
zones.supervision_hint: Silent longer than this is a fault; any report counts, even without a change. Set it longer than this sensor's own reporting interval. Empty: off, which is the default and right for sensors that report only when they change.
zones.bypassable_hint: Needed for automatic or forced exclusion.
zones.allow_faulted_hint: Arming proceeds even if this zone cannot be read. Leave off unless you know why.
zones.enabled_hint: A disabled zone is ignored completely.
zones.key_hint: A key arms or disarms as a person would. It never alarms.
zones.area_armed: This zone's area is armed: changes are refused until it is disarmed.
zones.follows_hint: Its own area's entry delay always counts. Tick the delayed zones of other areas whose entry delay it should also inherit, such as the front door for a hall sensor in an interior area.
zones.fire_statement: Foyer is not a fire alarm system. A smoke or gas detector connected to Home Assistant does not replace certified, interconnected smoke alarms.
zones.technical_hint: A technical zone raises the technical alarm whatever the areas are doing. It never triggers an area and disarming never clears it. Save it while the detector is quiet: a detector already detecting when saved counts as its starting point and alarms only once it has returned to normal and detects again.
zones.cross_zone_hint: Another zone that confirms this one within the window. Each still alarms on its own; when both detect, the pair is recorded as confirmed. Set it on either zone.
zones.trigger_count_hint: How many times it must detect within the window before it alarms. 1: at once. Only detections that would alarm at once are counted: opening the entry route is not.
zones.chime_hint: Plays the chime when it opens while its area is not armed.
zones.in_group: Member of the verification group {group}. Change it on the Verification groups page.
zones.bypass_hint: An excluded zone does not alarm. Without a duration it is included again when the area is disarmed; with one it is included again on its own, and says so.
zones.silent_hint: The response runs without the action kinds chosen in Settings, such as sirens.
zones.profile_hint: Read only when this zone alarms. Empty: the area's profile.
zones.battery_hint: For diagnostics and the low-battery warning. A low battery warns and never blocks arming; an entity that cannot be read at all is a fault and does block.
zones.cameras_hint: A notification set to show the zones' cameras sends these, in this order, one picture each after the text, and at most four cameras across the whole alarm.
zones.cameras_none_hint: No cameras: a notification set to show the zones' cameras sends its text alone when this zone alarms. Choose the camera that shows it, and the one in the room next door.

scenarios.mode_hint: What the Whole house panel reports to Home Assistant — and so to HomeKit, Google and Alexa — while this scenario is armed. Several scenarios may share one; the Whole house panel then refuses that mode and the scenario is chosen here.

scenarios.siren_hint: At most 900 s. Empty: the global setting.
scenarios.areas_hint: Only these are armed. Switching to another scenario disarms the areas it does not list.
scenarios.allowed_users_hint: Only the people ticked may use this scenario. Changing this list also needs the “Manage users and codes” permission.

help.global_toggle: Show or hide every help panel

overview.title: What this page shows
overview.intro: The live state of the alarm. It updates by itself; every button acts at once.

area.text: Arms and disarms on its own. Its button arms only that area.

master.text: Derived from the areas: armed if any is. Disarm here disarms everything.

scenario.text: Arms a set of areas. Chosen while another is armed, it takes its place.

not_ready.text: Open, faulted or excluded zones. Faults block arming unless the zone allows it.

memory.text: Shows which zones alarmed. It stays after the sirens stop, until the area is disarmed or armed again.

technical.text: Smoke, gas, water: its own channel. Disarming does not clear it; acknowledge it.

incident.text: Every zone of one alarm, acknowledged once.

areas.title: What an area is
areas.intro: A group of zones armed together, with its own state and alarm panel entity. Group by what you arm together — perimeter, interior day, interior night — not by room: that is what makes “dog at home, perimeter only” possible.

own_state.text: Each area arms, delays and alarms independently.

entry.text: Longer gives you more time to disarm, and an intruder the same.

exit.text: Zones still open when it ends are handled by their own “If open when arming” setting.

reports_as.text: What Home Assistant, HomeKit and voice assistants see. Behaviour is unchanged.

zones.title: What a zone is
zones.intro: One Home Assistant entity plus alarm semantics. The type is only a preset; the engine reads the fields.

trigger.text: Which state means an alarm. Get it wrong and the zone never fires.

type.text: Fills the fields below. Every field stays editable.

entry_mode.text: Instant alarms at once; delayed starts the entry delay; follower inherits it, and is instant when there is nothing to inherit.

arm_policy.text: Block names the zone; exclude includes it again once closed; ignore arms anyway.

hold.text: Waits for the door you leave by. Fails if it stays open past the limit.

always_on.text: Fires even when disarmed. Tamper and panic are always on.

supervision.text: A sensor that reports nothing for too long is a fault, never “all quiet”.

verification.text: Cross-zone verification and activations needed cut false alarms; a group does it for several zones.

cameras.text: The cameras that show this zone. A notification set to show the zones' cameras sends them when it alarms.

scenarios.title: What a scenario is
scenarios.intro: A named set of areas to arm together. Create as many as the house needs.

areas.text: Exactly these are armed by it.

reports_master.text: The mode HomeKit and voice assistants see. A mode shared by two scenarios cannot be armed from Whole house.

switching.text: Choosing another scenario while armed disarms the areas it does not list.

exit_override.text: Replaces each area's own for this scenario.

siren.text: A night scenario may sound for less. Never more than 900 s.

groups.title: What a verification group is
groups.intro: A group confirms an alarm when at least a set number of its member zones (the threshold) detect within a window: the strongest tool against false alarms in large spaces. Cross-zone verification on a zone works the same way, as a group of two where both must detect.

threshold.text: How many members, within how long. A longer window is easier to satisfy.

members.text: Any intrusion zone, in any area. Opening the entry route never counts.

suppress.text: Off by default: each member still alarms alone. On: nothing until the group is satisfied.

derived.text: Cross-zone pairs, shown here and edited on the zone.

settings.title: What these settings do
settings.intro: Settings that apply to the whole system: the chime, and where every response chain ends.

targets.text: Where the chime sounds. Nothing chimes until one is set.

mode.text: A sound, or the zone's name spoken, which tells you what opened.

quiet.text: No chime inside this window. A single speaker or siren may have a window of its own.

during_exit.text: Whether zones chime while their area counts down to armed.

response.text: The profile everything inherits, the one the technical channel uses, and what a silent zone keeps quiet.

retention.text: Per category, in days. A category switched off writes nothing from now on; rows already written stay until their days are up.

backup.text: A JSON file of the whole configuration. Restoring it goes through the same validation as any edit, and while an area is armed it is refused wherever the same change made on its own page would be.

alarmo.text: Brings Alarmo's areas, sensors, modes and people in beside what is here, after showing what it would do. Zones arrive switched off until you confirm them, and nobody arrives with a code.

language.text: The language of what Foyer sends out — notifications, the spoken zone name. This panel already follows each Home Assistant user's own language.

privacy.text: Replace names in rows older than a chosen number of days, and decide now whether removing Foyer should take the log database with it. The first costs you the answer to “who disarmed that night”.

armed.text: The siren, the delays, the response defaults and the camera folder keep the values the house was armed with. The language, the log, privacy, the chime and the backup download stay free.

profiles.title: What a response profile is
profiles.intro: A profile is a named list of actions: what happens, when, and under which conditions. The area is the unit of response; a zone's own profile is read only for its own alarm, which is what makes a verification group's graduated response work.

inheritance.text: Zone, then area, then scenario, then the global default. The page shows the profile in use and where it comes from.

moments.text: One action can answer several moments. Some moments arrive in a later version and are marked.

conditions.text: At most two per action, combined with and or or. More than that belongs in a Home Assistant automation.

severity.text: Only decides which escalation (the timed sequence of notifications) an incident follows when profiles of different strength contribute to it.

silent.text: A zone marked silent runs its response without the action kinds the settings name.

images.text: A notification can carry the cameras of the zones behind the alarm, one picture each after the text. Only at an alarm, never when somebody comes home.

armed.text: A profile the house could answer with cannot be changed until every area is disarmed: an armed area's own chain, the default, the technical channel's, and one an alarm is running on.

log.title: What is recorded, and for how long
log.intro: Stored in Foyer's own database rather than Home Assistant's recorder, whose ten-day purge would quietly destroy a thirty-day requirement. Every row records what happened, where, and through which channel.

category.text: Groups rows by kind. Each category is switched on or off, and kept for its own number of days, in Settings.

zone_disarmed.text: Off by default: one motion sensor produces thousands of rows a day and buries everything that matters. Switch it on while diagnosing, and off again afterwards.

incident.text: A real break-in trips several zones. They share one incident id, so a night reads as one story rather than as scattered rows.

user.text: The person is written into the row rather than referenced, so deleting a user later does not erase the history of what they did. Taking a person out of the log is a separate operation, on this page.

export.text: CSV or JSON of exactly the rows the filters above are showing — not of the whole database.

personal.text: Export every row about somebody, or take them out of the log without losing a single event. Erasing a person is not the same as deleting their account: the account goes, the history of what they did stays.

users.title: What this page decides
users.intro: Everyone has their own code, because a shared one makes “who disarmed at 03:14?” unanswerable. Codes are stored as hashes and checked only by Foyer on the server: a card is a keypad that transmits a code, never something that decides.

own_code.text: A code may not belong to two people. Change one and the log keeps every action the old one signed.

policy.text: Which operations ask for a code. An area or a scenario can ask for more; where they disagree, the one that asks wins. It cannot change while an area is armed; people and their codes can.

identified.term: Where a code can be skipped
identified.text: Only on channels that already know who you are. On a shared keypad the code is the identity, so the exemption cannot apply there.

duress.text: Works exactly as the ordinary code — arming, disarming, excluding, settings, anything — and every use raises a silent alarm that only the default profile answers. Nothing the person at the keypad can see is different.

lockout.text: Repeated wrong codes shut that keypad for a while, longer each time. It is also an event a response profile can answer: somebody guessing at a keypad is a tamper signal.

scope.text: A code can be limited to some areas or scenarios, and can stop working on a date — which is what makes a guest code a guest code. A walk test is the exception: it covers the whole house whatever areas are chosen.

devices.title: What this page decides
devices.intro: Any device that can call a service or publish to MQTT can arm this system and receives structured feedback for its LEDs, beeps and display. Keypad models change every few months; this contract does not. A device must be declared here before it may command anything.

declared.text: A device that is not on this page is refused, whatever code it brings, and the refusal is recorded and shown.

device_id.text: Recorded on every event, and what the lockout counts attempts against. Give each keypad its own.

identifies.text: A personal tag or badge identifies who acted, and needs no code. A shared keypad cannot, so the code is the only identity it has.

topics.text: Configurable, because people run more than one site against one broker and have a hierarchy they will not restructure.

detail.text: It is retained on a broker that is often shared, so it starts at the least a keypad needs and opens up only if you ask.

last_result.text: Lets a keypad distinguish a wrong code from arming blocked by an open window, instead of failing silently.

endpoint.text: A keypad can speak to Foyer's own endpoint with a token instead of MQTT, never both. The token proves which keypad it is; only HTTPS keeps the token and the codes from being read.

scopes.term: Permissions of a device on the endpoint
scopes.text: A display, a relay or a module reads and does only what is ticked for it, every permission off to begin with. Reading can be free; every action needs a code typed on the device.

test.title: What this page proves
test.intro: The point of an alarm you configured yourself is that you can check it before trusting it. The first two tabs only look: the table says what every zone is doing right now, and the simulator says what the house would do about it without doing any of it. The last two act: the walk test really arms the house and holds the response back, and the action test really sounds the siren.

trigger_column.text: Whether Foyer counts the zone as triggered right now, read through that zone's own trigger. A normally-closed contact alarms on “off”, so the raw state beside it is not the answer.

blocks.text: Whether this zone would stop its area arming, and which of the two reasons: a fault to fix, or a window to close.

battery.text: A low battery warns and never blocks: a door sensor at 15 % still works. A battery entity that cannot be read at all is a fault, and that one does block.

nothing_runs.text: The simulator runs the same engine the alarm runs and throws the result away. No siren, no notification, no change to what is armed.

clock.text: An action limited to 22:00–07:00 runs or does not run depending on this field. Set it to the hour you actually want to check.

skipped.term: Why an action did not run
skipped.text: Every action of the profile is listed, including the ones that were skipped, with the reason: a condition, a silent zone, a siren already sounding, or a delay still holding the rest of the sequence.

inherited.text: Zone, group, area, scenario or the global default. If a response looks arbitrary, this line is usually why.

walk_never.text: This is the finding, not the ones that did. A zone with no detection is either a door nobody opened or a PIR pointing at the wrong wall, and only you can tell which.

walk_timeout.text: Every detection pushes the timeout back so a large house can be walked in one pass, and an absolute cap ends it whatever happens. Neither can be switched off: while it runs, a real intrusion produces nothing.

walk_live.text: 24h, tamper, technical and panic zones respond in full, alarm included. A walk test never silences a smoke detector.

action_real.text: That is what makes it worth having: the failure it prevents is discovering during the emergency that the emergency channel was misconfigured. It asks first, and every run is in the log as a test rather than as an alarm.

contacts.title: What this page decides
contacts.intro: Escalation targets people, not services. Home Assistant already provides the transports — push, SMS, voice, messaging — so what is configured here is the order, the timing, and what counts as somebody having taken notice.

order.text: Tried highest first. Put the channel that survives a cut internet connection near the top, not at the bottom.

quiet.text: Only what is serious enough reaches this contact inside the window. It never suppresses an alarm for the rest of the household.

linked.text: Lets an acknowledgement from a phone be attributed to a person in the log.

step.text: A notification with a time on it, on the profile that answers the alarm. The escalation stops the moment anyone acknowledges.

acknowledge.text: Four paths stop the escalation, and each records who answered and how.

webhook.text: An unauthenticated URL that stops an alarm. Off until you switch it on, shown once when it is generated, and worth giving to nothing but the voice provider.

test.text: Really sends. Use it — an untested emergency channel is one you discover during the emergency.

armed.text: A contact that a profile the house could answer with notifies, at once or as a step, cannot be changed, switched off or deleted until every area is disarmed.

rules.title: What this page decides
rules.intro: A closed rule model, not an automation engine: four triggers, three actions, an active window and three safety checks. Rules act as a user would, so everything they do is logged with the rule's name — and everything a safety check stopped is logged too, because “why did it not arm last night?” is a question people ask.

trigger.text: Absence and entity state are conditions that stay true, so a rule a safety check blocked acts as soon as the check clears. A time or an arrival happens once: blocked, that occurrence is missed.

guards.text: Each one is a reason not to act. They are evaluated again when the countdown ends, because two minutes is long enough for somebody to come home.

grace.text: A notification with a Cancel button before the rule acts. Nobody presses anything and it happens; somebody presses Cancel and the rule waits until its condition becomes true again.

suspension.text: Holds rules back until a date and time, or for one occurrence. It is not a configuration change: it expires on its own.

visitor.text: The same suspension with a name on it. Mechanically identical; the difference is that the log still says why in six months.

disarming.text: Off until you turn it on, and never on a perimeter area. A scenario switch that would leave an armed area disarmed counts as disarming. It cannot change while an area is armed; a rule can always be switched off or suspended.

next.text: What is scheduled, not what will certainly happen: the safety checks are evaluated at the moment the rule acts, and the log says which one stopped it.

health.title: What system health watches
health.intro: An alarm that cannot tell you it has stopped working has stopped working. This page is the answer to the four failures that silently defeat a DIY alarm: the power goes out, the notification channel breaks, the radio goes quiet, or Home Assistant dies. None of it is an intrusion, and the one thing that ever reaches the alarm panel is interference confirmed on an armed house — which professional panels treat as tamper.

mains.text: Name the entity and which of its states means failure. A power cut is announced at once and is never a quiet night.

channels.text: The service is checked periodically; only a real send proves it delivers. A broken channel is announced over a different one.

watchdog.text: If Home Assistant dies the pings stop and the service you chose raises the alarm. Foyer also reports when it cannot reach it. Its URL is never shown again once saved.

payload.text: Off. On, the ping says how many areas are armed, which tells a third party when the house is empty.

radio.text: Zones are grouped by the integration they come from. Interference is suspected, never proven. Radios and thresholds cannot change while an area is armed.

coordinator.text: Without one, nothing is raised on that radio: it is what separates jamming from a dead coordinator.

diagnostics.text: Home Assistant's own download button, with everything personal removed and entity ids replaced.

api.title: What this page is for
api.intro: For whoever builds a device of the household's own — a touch display, a relay, an ESP32 or Arduino module. It shows, and lets you try, exactly what such a device may ask Foyer. Only Home Assistant administrators see it, and it is never served outside the panel: a public documentation page would tell a scanner that an alarm lives here.

contract.text: A device written against v1 keeps working: a change that would break it is a new version, and the changelog says so.

token.text: Generated on Arming devices and shown once. It says which device is asking; by itself it never arms or disarms anything, and it encrypts nothing.

try.text: Sends real requests with the token you paste, within that device's permissions. A section the device may not read answers 403 with the reason.

internal.text: The panel's own commands are internal and may change in any release: a device must not rely on them. The MQTT contract is described separately.

device_wrong_transport.message: Something used the name {device} over MQTT or a service call. That keypad speaks only through the device endpoint, with its own token, so the request was refused and nothing was changed. If it was not you, somebody knows the keypad's name.

token_lockout.title: Foyer: wrong tokens refused from one address
token_lockout.message: Too many requests with a wrong or missing token came from {address}. Until the lockout ends, a wrong or missing token from that address is refused. A device at that address with its right token keeps working, and its rows in the log say the address was locked. A keypad configured with an old token does this too; so does somebody guessing.

token_lockout_shared.title: Foyer: wrong tokens refused from many addresses
token_lockout_shared.message: Too many requests with a wrong or missing token came from more addresses than Foyer counts one by one, and those addresses share a single count. Until the lockout ends, a wrong or missing token from any of them is refused, and the refusals are counted in one log row a minute. A device with its right token keeps working. This many addresses usually means somebody guessing from a whole range of them.

auto_outcome_armed_later_switch.message: “{rule}” is switching to {scenario} now: the zones that were not ready are ready.

groups.title: Verification groups
groups.from_zone_hint: Cross-zone pairs appear here as 2-of-2 groups. They are edited on the zone, not here.
groups.members_hint: Intrusion zones of any area. A member counts only while its own area is armed, and only detections that would alarm at once count.
groups.suppress_hint: Off: each member still alarms on its own, and the group adds its confirmation. On: members do nothing until the group is satisfied — a single sensor facing a real intruder then produces silence.
groups.window_hint: Seconds within which the members must detect.
groups.no_zones: No intrusion zones available: each zone can be in one group or pair only.

settings.title: Settings
settings.chime_intro: Sounds when a zone with the chime switched on opens while its area is not armed — not merely when the house is disarmed. With only the perimeter armed, an internal door still chimes.
settings.targets_hint: Media players, sirens, and notify services or entities — the phone and Telegram chime too. Each one may have quiet hours of its own.
settings.no_targets: No media player or siren found.
settings.sound_hint: For media players: a media id or URL, such as media-source://media_source/local/chime.mp3. A siren sounds for one second, if it supports a set duration; otherwise it is skipped.
settings.tts_hint: Used to speak the zone name.
settings.volume_hint: Per cent. Empty: leave the player's volume as it is.
settings.quiet_hint: No chime in this window, which may cross midnight. Empty: never quiet.
settings.during_exit_hint: Off: the door you leave by does not chime while the area counts down.
settings.switch_hint: switch.foyer_chime silences it without changing these settings.
settings.response_intro: Where every inheritance chain ends, and what a silent zone keeps quiet.
settings.default_profile_hint: What every area, zone and scenario inherits unless it overrides it.
settings.technical_profile_hint: Smoke, gas and flood answer with this one, whatever the house is doing. Empty: the default profile.
settings.silent_hint: A zone marked silent runs its response without these.
settings.camera_dir_hint: Inside the configuration folder. Never www, which is served without authentication.
settings.defaults_intro: What new areas start with, and the limits that apply to every area.
settings.siren_duration_hint: How long sirens sound before stopping. Capped at 900 seconds, the EN 50131 reference for outdoor sirens; a disarm stops them sooner.
settings.arm_hold_hint: How long a zone set to “Arm after closing” may stay open once the exit delay is over. After that, arming fails as if the zone had blocked it.
settings.area_defaults_hint: Only for areas created from now on. Existing areas keep their own delays.
settings.log_intro: Which categories are recorded, and for how long each is kept.
settings.log_rows_hint: Rows already written stay until their days are up, even for a category you switch off.
settings.backup_intro: Nobody who has configured forty zones will do it twice.
settings.backup_hint: The file carries the schema version it was written with. A backup from an older version is brought up to date on restore; one from a newer version is refused rather than half-read.
settings.language_hint: This panel always follows the language of whoever is looking at it. This setting is for what Foyer sends out: notifications, and the zone name the chime speaks.
settings.low_battery_hint: Per cent. Below this a numeric battery counts as low. A battery binary sensor is read by its own “on” instead.
settings.walk_test_hint: Seconds a walk test runs without a detection before it ends itself. Each detection pushes it back, and an absolute cap ends it whatever happens. The automatic end is mandatory, so no value here switches it off.
settings.short_preset_hint: Sets {categories} to {days} days and leaves the rest alone. Offered for homes with domestic staff: those are the categories that name people, and the others carry faults and door states, which name nobody and are what you read when a sensor did not react three weeks ago.
settings.privacy_intro: The log is about people, and not only about whoever installed the system. These two settings apply to the whole system; erasing or exporting one person's rows is done on the log page.
settings.pseudonymise_warning: This trades away the ability to answer “who disarmed that night” for every row older than the delay — which is the very question the log exists to answer. It is a real trade, not a free safety feature. It runs once a day and cannot be undone: switching it off later brings no name back.
settings.pseudonymise_hint: Rows older than this keep a stable identifier instead of a name, so the shape of the nights survives and the names do not. Switching it on and switching it off are both recorded.
settings.delete_on_uninstall: Delete the log database if Foyer is removed
settings.delete_on_uninstall_hint: Off, removing Foyer leaves the database where it is, in the configuration directory, as foyer-log.db. Home Assistant's own confirmation is the last dialogue there is, so this is where the question gets answered — and keeping is the answer that destroys nothing.
settings.uninstall_snapshots_hint: Camera snapshots are never deleted with it. They are pictures of the inside of the house, in a folder you chose, which may hold files that are not Foyer's — so removing them is yours to do.
settings.pseudonymise_confirm: From the next start — and saving any setting is a start — every row older than {days} days loses the name on it, and the name inside its detail. It cannot be undone by switching this off again. The log will no longer answer who disarmed on those nights.
settings.defaults_armed: An area is armed: the siren time, how long arming waits for a zone to close, the default delays and the walk test timeout keep their values until every area is disarmed. The battery threshold can still be changed.
settings.response_armed: An area is armed: the default and technical profiles, what a silent zone keeps quiet and the camera folder keep their values until every area is disarmed.

moment.auto_arming_switched: Automatic rules switched on or off

condition.midnight_hint: A window may cross midnight: 22:00 to 07:00 is the night.
condition.max: At most two conditions per action. Anything more belongs in a Home Assistant automation subscribed to foyer_event.

profiles.title: Response profiles
profiles.intro: A profile is a reusable list of actions. It resolves by inheritance — zone, then area, then scenario, then the global default — which is what stops a house of sixteen zones turning into a configuration matrix.
profiles.severity_hint: Used for one thing only: when several zones join one incident, the incident adopts the escalation of the highest-severity profile among them. It changes nothing when this profile runs alone.
profiles.zone_hint: A zone's own profile is read only for its own alarm. Everything else in this area answers with the area's profile.
profiles.group_hint: What a satisfied group does. Its members keep their own profile: that is what makes the response graduated.
profiles.delay_hint: In seconds. It holds the actions after it in this list, and survives a restart.
profiles.revert_hint: In seconds. Empty: leave it as it is.
profiles.camera_hint: The notification attaches the live picture; the file is written to the camera folder.
profiles.call_service_hint: Anything Foyer does not model natively. Data is JSON.
profiles.escalation_later: An escalation step is a notification with a time on it: give one a delay from the alarm start, and it waits instead of firing at once. Who it reaches is set on the Contacts page.
profiles.attach_hint: The live picture goes with the notification, through Home Assistant's authenticated proxy. No file is written.
profiles.attach_hint_telegram: Telegram fetches the picture from outside the house, so a still is written to the camera folder and sent with the message. That folder must be in allowlist_external_dirs.
profiles.pick_or_type: Pick one, or type it: an integration that is not loaded right now is not in the list.
profiles.notify_hint: A notify service (the Companion app, Telegram) or a notify entity. Both work.
profiles.siren_duration_hint: In seconds. It is capped at the siren cutoff, so a siren never outlives the alarm.
profiles.no_contacts: No contacts yet. Add one on the Contacts page to notify a person rather than a service.
profiles.contacts_hint: Who this notification reaches. Choose contacts or a service, never both.
profiles.escalation_hint: Seconds from the start of the escalation. With a time here this notification becomes a step: it waits, and it stops the moment somebody acknowledges.
profiles.escalation_moment_hint: Only an alarm or a technical alarm can be escalated: they are the two that can be acknowledged.
profiles.images_text_alone: Pictures go only with an alarm: a trigger, a zone joining it, an escalation step, a technical alarm. For “{moments}” this notification sends its text alone. Never at the start of an entry delay, which is somebody coming home.
profiles.images_channels: Only push and chat channels receive the pictures. An SMS, a voice call or an “other” channel receives the text alone, rather than one more message per camera.
profiles.test_after_save: Save the profile to test this action as it is now: the test runs the saved one.
profiles.json_invalid: This is not valid JSON, so it was not kept. Correct it and leave the box.
profiles.duress_hint: Raised by every use of a duress code, whatever it was for. Only the default profile answers it, and it runs silent. Send it to somebody outside the house.
profiles.duress_not_default: This is not the default profile, so this action never answers a duress code.
profiles.duress_persistent: A Home Assistant notification shows on every Home Assistant screen, the wall tablet included — where the person who typed the duress code may be standing beside whoever made them. Send a notification to a contact instead.
profiles.duress_silent: {kind} is on the silent list, so it never runs for a duress code: a sound in the house would tell the room.

event_type.auto_arming_switched: Automatic rules switched on or off

log.categories_hint: Nothing selected means every category. Zone activity while disarmed is only recorded if you switch that category on in Settings.
log.clear_confirm: This deletes every row, for good. The deletion itself is recorded, so the log will not pretend nothing happened.
log.empty: Nothing recorded yet for these filters.
log.truncated: Exported {rows} rows of {total}. Narrow the filters to export the rest.
log.person_intro: The log records who was in the house and when, for as long as retention keeps it. Export hands somebody every row that is about them; erasing takes them out of the log and leaves every event where it is, so the record of what happened survives the removal of who.
log.person_found: Rows that would be erased: {total} — {by_id} found by their account, {by_name} by name alone (written before they were a Foyer user, or under a name they have since changed), {about} about their account.
log.person_export_rows: Rows in an export: {rows} — what they did, plus what the house did to them: their tag refused, an escalation that reached them.
log.person_erase_confirm: This empties the name, the account, the channel and the device on every row found — {rows} of them — for good. The events stay: the log will still say what happened that night, and will no longer say who. The erasure itself is recorded, without naming them.
log.person_erase_confirm_pseudonym: This replaces the name on every row found — {rows} of them — with a stable identifier, for good. The log will still say that the same person acted on two different nights, which is not the same as forgetting them. The erasure itself is recorded, without naming them.
log.person_keep_pseudonym: Keep a stable identifier instead of forgetting
log.person_keep_pseudonym_hint: Off, the rows lose the person entirely. On, they keep an opaque identifier that says nothing about them but still links their rows to each other. Somebody asking to be forgotten is usually asking for the first.
log.person_erased: Rows that no longer name anybody: {rows}.
log.tokens_rejected: {count} wrong tokens refused from {addresses} addresses sharing one lockout

alarmo.title: Import from Alarmo
alarmo.intro: Reads Alarmo's configuration from this Home Assistant and brings its areas, sensors, modes and people into Foyer, beside what is already here. It is a best-effort tool, not a migration: the file it reads is Alarmo's internal format, which may change in any Alarmo release without notice and without anybody being at fault, so it tells you everything it could not bring across. Nothing is written until you have read that and pressed Apply.
alarmo.report_title: What to know before you apply
alarmo.applied: Imported. Now give each person a code on the Users page, and confirm each zone on the Zones page before switching it on.
alarmo.hint: Until Foyer's zones are confirmed, keep Alarmo watching the house — but never arm both on the same sensors.

created.extended: Scenarios that would also arm what is brought in: {names}

setting.disarm_after_trigger: disarm when the siren time runs out

refused.not_found: There is no Alarmo configuration in this Home Assistant (.storage/alarmo.storage).
refused.unreadable: Alarmo's configuration file is there, but it could not be read.
refused.too_large: Alarmo's configuration file is far larger than any house needs, and was not read.
refused.not_json: Alarmo's configuration file is not valid JSON.
refused.not_alarmo: The file is not an Alarmo configuration.
refused.version_unsupported: This file is in Alarmo's storage format {version}, which this importer has not been checked against. It reads formats 6.1 to 6.3, written by Alarmo 1.9.5 to 1.10.19. Nothing was brought across.
refused.invalid: The file does not have the shape this importer was written for, at {where}. Rather than bring half of it across, it brought nothing.
refused.too_many: {where} has more than {limit} entries, which is not a house. Nothing was brought across.
refused.nothing_to_import: There is nothing in Alarmo's configuration that Foyer does not already have.
refused.changed: Something changed since the preview — Alarmo's file, Foyer's configuration or one of the sensors. Read it again, and look before applying.

line.codes: No code came across, and none ever will: Alarmo keeps its codes as hashes in its own format, and Foyer does not take a credential from another system on trust. Everybody brought in — {people} in all — needs a new code on the Users page before they can disarm with one.
line.codes_nobody: No code came across, and none ever will: Alarmo keeps its codes as hashes in its own format, and Foyer does not take a credential from another system on trust. Nobody new was brought in, so the people who can disarm are the ones already on the Users page.
line.zones_to_confirm: Zones brought in: {zones}, every one switched off. Each trigger is Foyer's proposal from the kind of sensor, not something anybody has checked: until you confirm it on the Zones page and switch the zone on, it watches nothing.
line.unavailable_is_fault: A sensor that goes unavailable is a fault in Foyer, never a quiet one: it blocks arming and is reported. Alarmo read it as closed unless told otherwise.
line.sensor_duplicate: {entity} is listed twice in the file; it was brought in once.
line.sensor_exists: {entity} is already Foyer's zone “{zone}”, which was left exactly as it is.
line.sensor_domain: {entity} is not a kind of entity Alarmo could see open or closed, so there was no zone to make of it.
line.sensor_no_area: {entity} belongs to an area that is not in the file, and was not brought in.
line.sensor_made_always_on: {entity} was a {type} sensor that was not always on in Alarmo. In Foyer it watches all the time, as that kind of sensor must.
line.sensor_no_mode: {entity} was not active in any mode its area had switched on, so Alarmo never watched it; it was not brought in.
line.entry_delay_varies: {entity} had a different entry delay in different modes. Foyer gives a zone one, and it took the longest: {seconds} s.
line.sensor_missing: {entity} does not exist in Home Assistant right now. The zone “{zone}” was made anyway, and will show as a fault until the entity is back.
line.trigger_unavailable: “{zone}” sounded the alarm in Alarmo when it became unavailable. In Foyer that is a fault: it blocks arming and is reported, but it does not sound.
line.delay_on: “{zone}” had to stay triggered {seconds} s before Alarmo acted on it. Foyer has no such wait and acts the first time; counting triggers on the zone is the nearest thing.
line.sensor_was_disabled: “{zone}” was switched off in Alarmo too. Confirming its trigger does not oblige you to switch it on.
line.delay_capped: “{item}” had a delay of {seconds} s. Foyer's maximum is {max} s, and that is what it has now.
line.area_empty: Alarmo's area “{area}” had no sensor left to bring in, so it did not become a Foyer area.
line.area_no_modes: Alarmo's area “{area}” had no mode switched on, so nothing in it was ever armed; it was not brought in.
line.renamed: {kind} named “{wanted}” already exists, so the new one is “{name}”.
line.exit_delay_varies: “{area}” had a different exit delay in different modes or areas. Foyer gives it one, and it took the longest, {seconds} s: a delay too short locks you out with the siren going.
line.area_split: Alarmo's area “{area}” became {areas}: its sensors were watched in different modes, and in Foyer a scenario arms whole areas.
line.arm_while_open: Sensors that Alarmo let you arm with open, as long as they were closed when the exit delay ran out: {zones}. In Foyer they must be closed when you press arm — or be set to arm after closing.
line.arm_on_close: “{zone}” armed the house five seconds after it closed, in Alarmo. In Foyer it is set to arm after closing, which also waits for the exit delay.
line.auto_bypass_partial: “{zone}” was excluded automatically in some modes and not in others. Foyer has one policy per zone, and it took the one that refuses to arm with the zone open.
line.mode_unused: The mode {mode} was switched on in Alarmo but watched no sensor that came across, so no scenario was made for it.
line.scenario_extended: Your scenario “{scenario}” already reports {mode} to Home Assistant, so it now also arms the areas brought in for that mode — a second scenario would make Whole house refuse it. Its own exit delay, siren duration and code settings apply to them.
line.scenario_mode_ambiguous: Two scenarios already report {mode}, so Whole house refuses that mode. A new one was made anyway, and Whole house refuses the mode until only one is left.
line.siren_varies: Alarmo's areas sounded for different times in this mode. “{scenario}” has one siren duration, and it took the longest: {seconds} s.
line.exit_abort: Sensors that stopped an arming in Alarmo the moment they opened during the exit delay: {zones}. Foyer checks them when you press arm and when the delay runs out, not in between.
line.scenario_restricted: Only some people may use “{scenario}”, and the people brought in are not among them until you add them on the Scenarios page.
line.profile_hides_scenario: “{area}” answers with its own response profile, so it no longer inherits the one “{scenario}” has. Check on the Response profiles page that it notifies whoever that one did.
line.automation_no_area: “{automation}” acted on an area that did not come across, and was not brought in.
line.automation_empty: “{automation}” had nothing to do, and was not brought in.
line.siren_not_imported: “{automation}” sounds a siren at another moment than the alarm, or with a tone or a duration of its own. Brought across, that would become the full siren for the full time, so it was not.
line.person_duplicate: {person} is in the file twice; they were brought in once.
line.siren_capped: Alarmo sounded for {seconds} s in this mode (0 means until somebody disarmed). Foyer's hard maximum is {max} s, so “{scenario}” sounds for {max} s.
line.person_unnamed: A person with no name in the file was not brought in.
line.person_exists: {person} is already a Foyer user, and was left exactly as they are.
line.override_code: {person} had an override code in Alarmo, which armed past open sensors. In Foyer that is the force-arm permission, and it was given.
line.person_scope_empty: {person} was limited to areas that did not come across, so for now they may use none; widen it on the Users page.
line.automation_disabled: The automation “{automation}” was switched off in Alarmo, and was not brought in.
line.automation_notification: The notification “{automation}” was not brought in. A notification that arrives somewhere unintended is worse than one you set up again: in Foyer, notifications go to contacts, on the Contacts page.
line.automation_trigger: “{automation}” starts on something Foyer's response profiles have no moment for, and was not brought in.
line.automation_modes: “{automation}” ran only in some modes. A Foyer profile answers for an area whatever the scenario, so it was not brought in.
line.action_not_imported: “{automation}” calls {service}, which is not a siren or a switch; that part was not brought in.
line.siren_off_not_needed: “{automation}” turned a siren off. Foyer does that itself when you disarm and when the siren time runs out, so it was not needed.
line.automation_imported: “{automation}” came across: its sirens and switches.
line.profile_created: The response profile “{profile}” starts as a copy of your default one, plus the sirens and switches from Alarmo, and answers for the areas brought in.
line.group_not_imported: The group “{group}” ({n} of {members} within {seconds} s) was not made: a group needs its members switched on, and every zone brought in starts switched off. Make it on the Verification groups page once they are confirmed.
line.setting_not_imported: Alarmo's setting “{setting}” was not brought across; Foyer's own settings were left as they are.
line.unknown_field: The file has a field this importer does not know: {field}. It was written by a newer Alarmo than the one this was checked against, and whatever that field does was not brought across.
line.scenario_overrides: “{scenario}” has its own exit delay or siren time, and it now applies to the imported areas too, whatever Alarmo had. Check it on the Scenarios page.

wizard.title: Finish setting up Foyer
wizard.intro: The integration created one area, one zone and one scenario — nothing is armed yet. Five short steps turn that into a setup that covers the whole house. You can stop at any point and carry on from the pages above.
wizard.no_area: No area found. Add one from the Areas page.
wizard.no_scenario: No scenario found. Add one from the Scenarios page.
wizard.area_text: One area is enough to start. More areas mean more partial arming later — the perimeter alone, or the ground floor with the dog at home.
wizard.exit_hint: How long you have to leave after arming.
wizard.entry_hint: How long you have to disarm after opening a delayed zone. Zones inherit this unless they say otherwise.
wizard.proposed: {name} is {state} right now. Foyer will treat it as in alarm when it is: {states}.
wizard.confirm_trigger: I tried it: opening or triggering it changes the state above to the one listed.
wizard.confirm_hint: This is the one thing Foyer cannot get right on its own. Normally-closed and normally-open contact sensors behave in opposite ways, and a wrong guess here produces an alarm that never fires — which you would find out at the worst possible moment.
wizard.scenario_text: A scenario is a named preset that arms a chosen set of areas. One that arms everything is enough to start; partial ones come later.
wizard.user_text: Your own code, so the log has somebody to credit from the first day.
wizard.test_text: Prove that a message actually reaches you before you rely on it. This goes through Foyer, as a real alarm message would, and is logged as a test.
wizard.test_sent: Sent. If nothing arrived, that channel would not have reached you during an alarm either.
wizard.test_hint: Which notifications Foyer sends, and when, is set on the Response profiles page.
wizard.test_message: Foyer Home Defender: this is a test notification.
wizard.user_hint: This person is linked to your Home Assistant account and gets every permission — you are the one setting the system up. Everyone else is added on the Users page, each with their own code.
wizard.user_done: {name} holds a code. From now on disarming asks for one.
wizard.numeric_elsewhere: This sensor reports a number: set its threshold on the Zones page.
wizard.type_hint: Instant sounds the alarm at once. Delayed leaves the entry delay to disarm: for the door you come in by.
wizard.type_fixed: Zone type: {type}. It can be changed on the Zones page.

users.title: Users
users.none: No users yet. Until somebody holds a code, anyone who can reach Home Assistant can disarm.
users.not_enforced_hint: No user holds a code, so no code is ever asked for. Create a user with a code and the policy below starts applying at once.
users.code_hint: {n} digits, and it may not be anybody else's. Leave it empty to keep the current one.
users.duress_hint: Works exactly as the ordinary code, for anything it is used for, and each time raises a silent alarm that only the default profile answers. Nothing visible changes.
users.linked_hint: Linking a Home Assistant account lets the panel know who is acting without a code being typed.
users.validity_hint: For a guest code: outside this window the code is refused.
users.exempt: Skip the code where this person is identified
users.exempt_hint: Only on channels that identify the person by themselves — the Home Assistant UI of their own account.
users.exempt_note: On a shared keypad the code is the identity: the system cannot know who is typing until they type. The exemption never applies there. And a tablet left signed in as this person is a disarm anybody passing can press.
users.enabled_hint: A disabled user's code is refused, and their history is kept.
users.policy_hint: Which operations ask for a code. Areas and scenarios can ask for more, never for less.
users.code_length_hint: The same for everybody, because a keypad has to know how many digits to collect. Four digits is ten thousand combinations: it leans entirely on the lockout below.
users.lockout_hint: Each further lockout from the same source lasts twice as long. The Home Assistant admin path is never locked, so nobody can shut themselves out.
users.confirm_delete: Delete {name}? This cannot be undone. Their code stops working at once; their history stays in the log.
users.policy_armed: An area is armed: the code policy, the code length and the lockout keep their values until every area is disarmed. People and their codes can still be changed.
users.walk_test_note: Walk test covers the whole house, whatever areas are chosen below. It arms every disarmed area it can, and until it ends no area answers an ordinary detection — one somebody else armed included — for up to three hours. Whoever holds it can keep an armed house quiet without Disarm, so give it as you would give Disarm.

devices.title: Arming devices
devices.none: No arming device yet. A keypad, a tag or a remote is declared here before it may command anything.
devices.white_list: This list is a white list, not an address book: a device that is not here is refused whatever code it brings. That is what lets the lockout count attempts, because a caller free to invent a device name is a caller who is never locked out.
devices.kind_hint_keypad: Shared, and carries a code. On a shared keypad the code is the identity, so the per-user exemption can never apply here.
devices.kind_hint_tag: One person's, and carries no code at all: an NFC tag, an RFID badge, a remote.
devices.ref_hint: The name this keypad puts in its own messages, in device_id. It is recorded on every event and is what the lockout counts attempts against, so give each keypad its own.
devices.stolen_tag: A stolen tag arms and disarms without knowing any code.
devices.stolen_tag_hint: Possession is the credential: there is nowhere to type a code on a tag. Keep it as you would keep a key, and give it to somebody you would give a key to. Everything else about that person still applies: what they may do, which areas, and until when.
devices.entity_hint: The tag or event entity a scan arrives on. Scan the tag once with Home Assistant to make it appear.
devices.event_type_hint: For a remote with more than one button: which event counts. Leave it empty for a tag, which has only the scan.
devices.owner_hint: Whose tag this is. This is the whole of its identity, and what the log will say.
devices.enabled_hint: Switched off, it stops commanding, not merely disappearing from this list.
devices.mqtt_note: Keypad models churn every six months; this contract does not. Anything that can publish to a broker can arm this house, and gets structured feedback back for its LEDs and beeps. Everything here is also available as the foyer.* services, for a device that cannot publish MQTT.
devices.mqtt_enabled: Listen and publish on the broker
devices.mqtt_enabled_hint: Off until you switch it on: a broker is often somebody else's machine.
devices.topic_hint: Leave empty for the default, foyer/<install id>/command. People run more than one site against one broker.
devices.detail_hint_minimal: What a keypad needs and nothing else: no scenario name, no area names, no list of open windows.
devices.detail_hint_standard: Adds the active scenario and the state of each area, by name.
devices.detail_hint_full: The contract as written, open zones by name included. Remember what “retained” means on a shared broker.
devices.retain_hint: Retained, so a keypad that reboots knows the state without asking, and so does anyone else who connects to the broker afterwards.
devices.last_result_hint: last_result is what lets a keypad tell a wrong code from arming blocked by an open window, instead of failing silently.
devices.ref_hint_http: The name this keypad is recorded under. On the endpoint the token is its identity, and this name is refused over MQTT and in service calls, so that knowing it gets nobody round the token.
devices.transport_hint_mqtt: The broker: the keypad is the name it gives. Anybody who can publish to the topic can use that name.
devices.transport_hint_http: Foyer's own endpoint, with a token for this keypad alone. One or the other, never both: on the endpoint its name is refused everywhere else.
devices.in_clear: This keypad is talking in the clear.
devices.in_clear_hint: Its last request reached Home Assistant unencrypted. Its token and every code typed on it can be read by anybody on the network in between. Serve Home Assistant over HTTPS, or through a reverse proxy it trusts, and this warning goes the moment a request arrives encrypted.
devices.token_note: The token authenticates the keypad; it does not encrypt anything. A stolen token disarms nothing without a code, and the code is still the identity of whoever typed it.
devices.token_once_hint: Copy it into the keypad now. Foyer keeps only a fingerprint of it and cannot show it again; if it is lost, generate a new one.
devices.token_save_first: Save the keypad on the endpoint first; then its token can be generated here.
devices.token_exists: This keypad has a token. It cannot be shown again: a new one replaces it at once and closes every connection the old one had open.
devices.token_none: No token yet: this keypad cannot reach the endpoint until one is generated.
devices.endpoint_stream_hint: The same message as MQTT's, at the same detail level, the moment anything changes; a comment line every thirty seconds keeps the connection open through proxies.
devices.detail_shared_hint: The same level applies to the device endpoint's state stream and to its answers.
devices.token_dropped: Saving it on MQTT revokes its token. Back on the endpoint it will need a new one.
devices.token_confirm: The keypad stops working with its current token at once, and every connection it has open is closed.
devices.scopes_note: A display in the hall, a relay that lights an “armed” lamp, a module of your own: a device on the endpoint may do exactly what is ticked here and nothing more, whatever code is typed on it. Everything starts off.
devices.scopes_none: Nothing is ticked: this device reaches the endpoint and can do nothing at all.
devices.scopes_read_hint: Readable without a code: anybody standing at the device can read it. Otherwise it is read only for a while after somebody types a valid code on the device, and only what that person may see.
devices.scopes_act_hint: Every action needs a code typed on the device, arming included, even where the house would arm without one elsewhere: the token alone never arms or disarms anything. The action is made in the name of whoever the code belongs to, within what that person may do, and never beyond what is ticked here.

scope_hint.status: Armed or not, which scenario, the countdowns, whether it is ready to arm, an alarm. Enough for a lamp that lights when the house is armed.
scope_hint.zones: Every zone and its state: open, closed, in fault, excluded. Which window is open is exactly what a burglar wants to know.
scope_hint.batteries: Battery levels and tamper, per zone and per device.
scope_hint.health: Mains power, the notification channels, the watchdog, the radios.
scope_hint.log: The log, newest first, a page at a time. Names appear only after the code of somebody allowed to view the log.
scope_hint.arm: Arm a scenario or an area, within the limits chosen below.
scope_hint.disarm: Disarm, within the areas chosen below.
scope_hint.exclude: Exclude a zone from the next arming, and include it again.
scope_hint.acknowledge: Acknowledge an alarm or a technical alarm.

devices.free_log_hint: Without a code the log shows events with nobody's name in them.
devices.unlock_hint: From 30 seconds to 10 minutes, counted from the last time the device was used. It ends at once whenever the house is armed or disarmed from this device, and every unlock leaves a line in the log.
devices.reach_all_scenarios: Every scenario, as far as the code allows
devices.reach_whole_house: Whole house, as far as the code allows
devices.reach_none: Nothing is ticked, so it may not do this anywhere.
devices.clear_text_hint: If this device talks plain HTTP, everything these permissions read — and the codes typed on it — crosses the network readable by anybody in between. Over plain HTTP Foyer gives these readings only once this is ticked; over HTTPS it changes nothing. Ticking it leaves a line in the log.
devices.clear_text_now: Its last request arrived unencrypted: until this is ticked, it reads nothing beyond the state of the alarm.

simulator.safe: The simulator calls the same decision engine the alarm calls, with a made-up world and a made-up clock, and then simply never hands the result to whatever would run the sirens.
simulator.scenario_hint: The house is armed with this before anything else happens.
simulator.clock_hint: What a time condition is read against. Empty means now.
simulator.zones_hint: Each one happens this many seconds after the house has finished arming — so zero means “armed, and then this”. The delay is what lets you watch a group fill up, or a second zone join an alarm.
simulator.at: Seconds after the house is armed
simulator.entities_hint: Only the entities an action's conditions read. Leave one empty to use what it really says right now.
simulator.premise_code: This system asks for a code to arm, and the simulation arms the house before anything else happens — so it asks for one too. Nothing is executed either way.

walk.banner: Every response is held back. It ends in {time}, or when you end it. Started by {who}.
walk.card_banner: The alarm will not sound. Ends in {time}.
walk.badge_title: A walk test is running: the alarm will not sound.
walk.always_on_live: 24h, tamper, technical and panic zones stay fully live. A walk test never silences a smoke detector.
walk.idle: Starting a walk test really arms the house and really reads the sensors. What is held back is the response: no siren, no notification, no light.
walk.active: Walk the house. The table below fills in as zones detect you, and the ones that never do are the finding.
walk.start_sub: Really armed, really reading, nothing answering
walk.explainer: Every disarmed area that can arm is armed — the whole house, whatever areas you are allowed otherwise — except one still holding alarm memory, whose zones still record you walking past. An area a zone is holding open stays out, and is named. One that was already armed stays armed, and does not answer either until the test ends. The end disarms the areas the test armed, except one in alarm.
walk.duration_hint: Minutes without a detection before it ends itself. Each detection pushes it back. It can only be shorter than the system setting, never longer: the automatic end cannot be switched off.
walk.never_reacted: {n} zones have not reacted yet. A door nobody opened reads the same as a PIR pointing at the wrong wall — walk them again before you trust the list.
walk.all_reacted: Every zone under test has detected you at least once.
walk.partly_armed: The walk test is running, but these zones kept their area out of it: {zones}. Those areas were never armed, so their zones cannot detect anything.
walk.never_reacted_one: One zone has not reacted yet. A door nobody opened reads the same as a PIR pointing at the wrong wall — walk it again before you trust the list.

action_test.warn: Sirens really sound and messages really send. That is the point: an emergency channel discovered broken during the emergency is what this page exists to prevent. Every run is recorded in the log as a test.
action_test.subtitle: One button per action, and it really runs
action_test.no_profiles: No response profiles yet. Create one under Response profiles.
action_test.no_actions: This profile has no action to test.
action_test.confirm: Really run “{action}” now? It executes for real.

what.delay: Nothing: a delay is the waiting itself

contacts.title: Contacts
contacts.none: No contacts yet. An escalation reaches people, so it needs at least one.
contacts.channels_hint: Tried highest first. Put the channel that survives a cut internet connection somewhere in the list, not at the bottom.
contacts.service_hint: Any notify service or notify entity in this Home Assistant. Foyer orchestrates transports; it does not implement them.
contacts.target_hint: What this transport needs to reach the person: a phone number, a chat id. Leave it empty when the service already knows.
contacts.actionable_hint: The Companion app can; an SMS cannot. A transport throws away a key it does not know without a word, so this is declared rather than guessed.
contacts.quiet_hint: Inside this window only what is serious enough reaches this contact. It never silences the alarm for the rest of the household.
contacts.quiet_severity_hint: On the log's own scale. Left at alarm, a break-in gets through at four in the morning and a successful arming does not.
contacts.linked_hint: Lets an acknowledgement from this person's phone be attributed to them in the log.
contacts.orchestration: Escalation targets people, not services. Home Assistant already provides the transports, so what is configured here is who, in what order, and when to stop.
contacts.test_after_save: Save the contact first: a test sends through the stored channel, not the draft.
contacts.no_policies: No escalation steps yet. A step is a notification with a time on it, added to a response profile.
contacts.exhausted: If nobody acknowledges, the last step raises escalation_exhausted, which is itself a moment a profile can act on.
contacts.ack_stops: The escalation stops the instant any of these arrives. Every acknowledgement records who and through which channel.
contacts.ack_push: Action button in a push notification
contacts.ack_push_how: A channel marked as able to carry one
contacts.ack_disarm_how: Keypad, card, tag, service call — an area the alarm touched
contacts.ack_dtmf: Key press during a voice call
contacts.ack_dtmf_how: Captured by the provider, fed back to the webhook below
contacts.webhook_enable: Accept an acknowledgement from a webhook
contacts.webhook_warning: This URL stops an alarm, and nothing authenticates it.
contacts.webhook_warning_hint: Home Assistant webhooks are open to whoever holds the address: anybody who has it, or intercepts it, can stop the escalation on its way to your neighbour. Switch it on only if a voice provider needs it, and give the address to nothing else.
contacts.webhook_hint: The voice provider posts to the webhook's address when the key is pressed: give it to the provider and to nothing else. Switching the webhook off forgets the address; switching it on again gives out a new one.
contacts.actionable_entity: This is a notify entity: it carries a message and a title and nothing else, so no button, no target and no extra data reach the phone. Use the notify service behind it if this channel should be able to acknowledge.
contacts.webhook_once_hint: Copy it into the voice provider now. Foyer cannot show it again; if it is lost, generate a new one.
contacts.webhook_path_hint: Home Assistant knows no external address, so this is the path alone: put in front of it the address your Home Assistant is reached at from the internet.
contacts.webhook_exists: The webhook is on. Its address cannot be shown again. If you need it, generate a new address: the old one stops working at once.
contacts.webhook_confirm: The address the voice provider holds stops working at once, and it will need the new one.
contacts.webhook_copy_failed: This browser would not copy it: select the address and copy it by hand.

rules.title: Automatic rules
rules.none: No rules yet. The house arms itself only once one exists.
rules.switched_off: Automatic rules are switched off. Nothing will arm or disarm on its own.
rules.trigger_absence: Everyone away for {minutes} min · people watched: {n}
rules.trigger_hint_absence: Every person chosen has to be away for the whole time.
rules.trigger_hint_presence: Fires when one of them comes home. Somebody already at home has not arrived.
rules.trigger_hint_time: Happens once. Blocked by a safety check, the occurrence is missed rather than postponed.
rules.trigger_hint_entity: The entity has to hold that state for the whole time.
rules.no_people: No person or device tracker entities were found.
rules.people_hint: A person Home Assistant cannot read is never taken as evidence that nobody is in.
rules.window_hint: Outside this window the rule does not exist: it is not blocked and nothing is logged.
rules.guard_ready: Only if every zone is ready
rules.guard_ready_hint: Otherwise the rule would arm around an open window.
rules.guard_quiet_label: Only if no interior motion for (minutes)
rules.guard_quiet_hint: Catches the flat phone battery: somebody is in, their phone is not.
rules.grace_hint: A notification with a Cancel button before it acts. 0 acts at once.
rules.notify_hint: Who hears the countdown and holds the Cancel button. Their quiet hours still apply.
rules.visitor_intro: A named window suspends automatic rules — and in six months the log says why, which a bare suspension never will.
rules.suspension_next_hint: Ends the next time the rule would have acted.
rules.instead_hint: Applied when the suspended rule would have armed, not when the window opens.
rules.disarming_warning: Presence is inferred from a phone. A stolen phone disarms the house, GPS drift of 200 metres disarms the house, a cloned MAC address on the home network disarms the house. This is the most banal attack against a DIY alarm, which is why this is off by default.
rules.allow_disarm_hint: Also covers a scenario switch that would leave an armed area disarmed.
rules.perimeter_note: Perimeter areas are left out by the engine itself, not by this screen. Whoever walks in on a stolen phone still finds every external door and window armed.
rules.block_not_ready_refused: Refused: a zone was not ready
rules.block_unknown_area: An area it names no longer exists
rules.exclude_open_hint: Only zones that are open and may be excluded. A zone in fault, or one that may not be excluded, still stops the arming. An excluded zone is watched again as soon as it closes.
rules.exclude_open_warning: This is a forced arming nobody types a code for: the house arms with that window uncovered. The countdown and the message afterwards name what was excluded.
rules.exclude_open_no_effect: With “only if every zone is ready” on, the rule never starts while a zone is open, so this has no effect.
rules.notify_outcome_hint: They receive the countdown, and a second message when the arming did not go as announced: not armed and why, armed later, or armed with zones excluded. That one reaches them even in their quiet hours.
rules.allow_disarm_armed: An area is armed: whether rules may disarm cannot change until every area is disarmed. A rule can still be switched off or suspended, and the global switch still stops them all.

health.settings_hint: Which entity reports the mains, where the watchdog pings, and which radios are counted together. Changing any of it is a configuration edit.
health.mains_hint: A UPS over NUT or a smart plug already gives you one. If it is also a zone of type technical, it keeps its own alarm and its own acknowledgement — this only tells Foyer which one is the mains.
health.mains_states_hint: Which states mean the mains has failed, separated by commas. A UPS binary sensor is usually “on” for a failure and a power sensor “off”: a wrong answer here is an alarm that never fires.
health.watchdog_off_hint: Nothing outside the house knows whether Foyer is alive
health.watchdog_note: Foyer watches the watchdog too: repeated failures to reach this endpoint are reported here, because being unable to reach the internet means no internet notification would go out either.
health.url_hint: healthchecks.io, Uptime Kuma, Cronitor, or anything that answers. If Home Assistant dies the pings stop and that service raises the alarm — the only answer to a dead system being unable to report its own death.
health.interval_hint: Seconds between pings. Shorter means the outside world learns sooner that Home Assistant has died.
health.failures_hint: How many pings in a row must fail before Foyer says so here.
health.payload: Include the state of the house in the ping
health.payload_warning: A ping that says “armed, nobody home” tells whoever runs that service exactly when your house is empty. Even switched on, Foyer sends only how many areas are armed — never which scenario, which areas, or which zones are open.
health.channels_note: A broken channel is announced through a different one, since a warning sent over the broken channel would never arrive. Send a test from the Contacts page.
health.no_radios: No radios are configured, so correlated silence is not counted.
health.radios_hint: A radio is one integration's config entry: every zone of one ZHA, Z-Wave JS or Zigbee2MQTT network shares it, so naming the entry once assigns forty zones.
health.radios_note: Many zones on one radio going quiet within seconds is the signature of jamming — and of a coordinator crash, a firmware update, a channel change and a power cut to a room of mains-powered routers. That is why the event is called suspected.
health.entry_hint: Only integrations that back at least one of your zones.
health.coordinator_hint: The gate that makes this worth having: zones going quiet while the coordinator answers is interference, zones going quiet with the coordinator gone is a dead coordinator. Without one, Foyer raises nothing on this radio rather than guessing.
health.rf_zones_hint: Or 40% of that radio's zones, whichever is lower.
health.rf_confirm_hint: How long the silence must last before Foyer says so. This is what a coordinator reboot and a firmware update walk into instead of the siren.
health.faults_sub: also shown in Home Assistant's Repairs
health.diagnostics_hint: An anonymised dump of the configuration and the state: no codes, no hashes, no personal names, no URLs, and entity ids reduced to stable placeholders. It is what turns a bug report into something answerable.
health.diagnostics_where: The download button is Home Assistant's own, on the integration's page, and it is available to administrators.
health.url_set_placeholder: Set — type a new URL to replace it
health.url_set_hint: A URL is saved. Foyer never shows it again, because whoever holds it can keep the check green for ever. Leave the field empty to keep it, or type the whole URL again to correct it.
health.radios_armed: An area is armed: the radios and the thresholds keep their values until every area is disarmed. The mains, the watchdog and the channel checks can still be changed.

images.zone: The cameras of the zones behind the alarm
images.zone_hint: Every zone in the alarm, in the order they alarmed, each camera once, at most four. The text goes first, with its buttons; then one notification per camera.
images.fixed_hint: The one camera chosen below, attached to the notification itself, whatever raised it.

api.title: Device API
api.intro: The contract of the device endpoint: what a display, a relay or a module on your network may ask Foyer, and what it answers. It describes the endpoint and its state stream and nothing else — the panel's own commands are internal and are not listed. Nothing on this page is fetched from the internet.
api.try_it: To try a request, press Authorize and paste the token of a device declared on Arming devices, then Try it out. The token stays in this page only: it is not saved in the browser, and it is forgotten when you leave.
api.real_requests: These are real requests to this house, made as that device: an arming or a disarming with a real code really arms or disarms it, a wrong code counts towards the device's lockout, and every action is recorded in the log.
api.failed: The contract could not be read from Home Assistant.
